title: The Third Wave: ARTEX and Agentic Offensive Frameworks (AOFs)
description: A draft briefing on agentic cyberattacks, with a risk register, defensive controls, and decisions for boards.

I. Executive Summary

The third wave of AI-driven cybersecurity threats has arrived with the emergence of Agentic Offensive Frameworks (AOFs) such as ARTEX and Cairn. Defined as autonomous software systems used for cyber attacks, powered by AI reasoning models, AOFs have reached privileged access in under three hours in some intrusions and are able to systematically probe attack surfaces, chain vulnerabilities, and perform concurrent internal network pivots rapidly.

While these attacks have been theoretically possible before, we have now seen them deployed by threat actors, at scale. The ability to leverage off-the-shelf frameworks alongside inexpensive, open-source reasoning models means that they are no longer limited to nation-state attackers but can be executed by very low-resourced criminals, increasing both the frequency and range of targets, as highlighted by numerous examples such as those below:

  • Check Point Research documented three ARTEX cybercrime campaigns run on DeepSeek and Kimi models at estimated model costs between $145 and $1,500.
  • SentinelOne counts at least five actors and clusters using ARTEX since late August, from China-nexus espionage groups to a Cambodia-based criminal cluster.

This fundamental change to the economics of cyberattacks will require organizations to accept new tradeoffs between operational control and cyber security. Recent events have proven that these tradeoffs are necessary to maintain board-level expectations of normal business operations while under an active, parallel, automated attack.

To effectively defend against these new threats, organizations must build an AI-storm-ready cybersecurity program:

  1. Traditional human-in-the-loop approvals cannot match AOF velocity, requiring security teams to deploy autonomous defensive agents governed by pre-approved containment policies. However, these autonomous agents must be carefully tested and matured to effectively balance rapid defense against the risk of accidental operational outages. Operating effectively under this model requires executive leadership to formally adopt and align with this paradigm shift.
  2. CISOs must be granted expanded authority and pre-approved decision rights, backed by an approved risk-planning framework and organizational approval, to immediately isolate, contain, or shut down compromised production systems when necessary, limit blast radius, and prevent rapid re-entry.
  3. Organizations must be willing to quickly identify, acquire, and integrate new security tools, even at the cost of increased operational thrash and higher costs.

Critical summary:

Even after these changes are implemented, we should expect that rapid technological advancements will require us to revisit when and how agents can make decisions, and how we build the guardrails to allow agents to make these decisions.

CISO Action Items

Defending against AOF campaigns requires automated security operations, continuous exposure validation, and resilient architectural controls. CISOs and executive boards must prioritize the following strategic imperatives:

CISOs must immediately perform these 4 steps in their organization: (1) Harden existing environment controls and reduce existing attack surface, (2) Employ and leverage agent capabilities as part of your workforce to operate at speeds, scales, and precision unreachable through human effort alone, (3) Expand agentic capabilities to be independent and autonomous across security functions, not limited to operations, (4) Move faster, deploy quicker, and maintain modern, dynamic governance to adopt new technologies on a 2-4 week cycle.

1. Hardened Defenses

Security programs must first establish operational controls to shrink external attack surfaces, validate via offensive testing, harden security infrastructure, and enforce total evictions.

2. Combine human expertise and AI agents

Automated attacks require people and agents to work in concert across discovery, triage, and action. Deploy agents to continuously discover vulnerabilities and anomalies, perform initial alert triage, and execute well-defined automated tasks. Concurrently, ensure that agents are strictly secured and monitored.

3. Expand Agent Capabilities for Autonomous Security Operations

Building directly upon human-AI collaboration, security teams must extend AI agents beyond investigation and alert triage to operate independently and autonomously across response, visualization, and governance workflows. Concurrently, ensure that agents are strictly secured and monitored.

4. Dynamic Governance

Supporting continuous agent implementation and autonomous operations, organizations must build the capacity to move faster, deploy quicker, and maintain modern, dynamic governance to adopt new technologies on a 2-4 week cycle.

Our immediate goal should be to adopt technologies early and shorten the adoption cycles. Longer term, organizations should focus on implementing controls as they mature across the industry, such as tested agentic response, automated SOC capabilities, and secured defensive agents.

Specifically, human-in-the-loop approval workflows cannot match AOF execution velocity. Establish delegated decision rights for automated containment.

II. Background

For the past two months, autonomous attacks have been seen across many organizations worldwide, using Agentic Offensive Frameworks (AOFs) such as ARTEX and Cairn. On November 13, 2026, the FBI issued FLASH-20261113-001 on ARTEX.

An AOF is an autonomous software system that uses AI reasoning models to run an intrusion campaign end to end, from a high-level objective stated in natural language. An operator gives the framework a target and an objective. It plans the work, runs standard tools, and tries another route when one fails, using whichever model the operator connects. The FBI describes some intrusions that reached privileged access in under three hours.

In April, The AI Vulnerability Storm warned that "Mythos is only the first wave of future AI technology disruptions." The first wave showed that a frontier model could find vulnerabilities and write working exploits faster than human teams. The second wave came in July, when an autonomous attack ran end to end against Hugging Face's production infrastructure with no attacker directing it. An earlier case, GTG-1002, was disclosed in November 2025. It ran on one vendor's model, and that vendor disrupted it. The third wave is adversaries running autonomous campaigns against production environments with downloadable frameworks and inexpensive, sometimes abliterated, models. About six months separate the Core Collapse warning from the first of these campaigns, and about nine separate it from the FBI alert.

Four days after the FBI alert, CSA convened more than 800 CISOs for an emergency briefing where some participants had already been compromised by these tools and shared their own learnings. For the first time in this series, we can report what participants saw work, and fail, against real adversaries.

These campaigns also test the assumptions behind how security programs are built and run. The controls and playbooks in this brief are practical steps toward building an “AI-storm”-ready security program as it evolves with this latest wave.

The tooling will keep changing, and within months a prompt is likely to do what a framework does today. Our goal is to lay out what we know now about building a security program for these attacks, while preparing not just against the current wave, but future waves.

III. Top Three Risks and Controls

Each control below answers the risk beside it. The full lists are in Section VI.

These controls fall into two groups. Attack surface management and red teaming are controls most organizations already have and can repurpose now. Wide adoption of agents, securing agents, and deception are deeper controls that keep working when the tooling changes.

ARTEX artifacts will age quickly, because new frameworks keep appearing, and within months a simple prompt is likely to replace the need for these frameworks. Faster patching is still necessary, and we already know it will not be enough for the next wave. Attack surface guidance is familiar. The threshold for exploitation is what changed. Paths that were impractical for a human attacker are practical for an AOF.

IV. What Survived the First Two Waves

The AI Vulnerability Storm and the Hugging Face post-mortem were written before adversaries ran autonomous campaigns at scale with downloadable frameworks. Most of their guidance held.

Affected parties report that enabling their people with agents was necessary. We'd now expand this advice to cover agents working across security functions themselves, rather than staff operating them.

The core imbalance of cybersecurity remained true: defenders must protect every possible entrance, while an attacker only needs to find a single open door.

The agent behaviors seen at Hugging Face appeared again: parallel bursts, immediate retries, paths no human would take, and poor operational security.

An organization's own agents still cause incidents. One large provider reported that some of its most notable incidents this year came from its own agents.

Deception slowed attackers in the cases participants described, as both papers recommended.

Credentials are usually the objective.

Cleaning a compromised environment in place often fails. Organizations that remediated partially were re-compromised within hours.

Defenders need cyber-capable models and a fallback. Responders with approved access were still refused during investigations.

V. What Is New in the Third Wave

Real adversaries now run these campaigns with commodity tooling. A campaign outcome now says little about the operator’s expertise, and targets once considered too low-value are in range. At least five actors and clusters have been named publicly (SentinelOne), and public reporting puts the model cost of observed campaigns between $145 and $1,500 (Check Point).

The campaigns still have limits. They rely mostly on known techniques, but use of vulnerability discovery and exploitation has been observed, including in third-party software. Reconnaissance is noisy and easy to detect. Exploitation was quieter: in one incident, a WAF that stopped the reconnaissance missed the breach.

In some of the reported incidents, the AOFs ran as small teams of agents (seven to ten).

  • Community contributors report attacks happening simultaneously across multiple sites and regions, within moments of each other. One participant saw activity surface on separate attack surfaces in the same minute from a single IP address. Lateral movement runs along several paths at once. Many response teams are built for one incident, or a few at most.
  • Faster patching is necessary, but not enough. One AOF lost its foothold and returned hours later through a second flaw. Another exploited a vulnerability before details of the flaw were public. Contributors also report agents analyzing newly released patches to build exploits for systems that have not applied them, including third-party systems.
  • Vulnerability hunting has no finish line. Repeated model runs can surface new potential vulnerabilities faster than teams can assess them manually. Invest in VulnOps that scales discovery, validation, prioritization, and remediation, while limiting the impact of remaining exposures through least privilege and service isolation.

New measures from the community:

Pre-approved actions

Per-action human approval cannot keep pace with a fast AOF. Several participants now approve defined classes of action in advance.

Response injection

One responder reported an approximately 18-hour pause after changing edge responses to tell the attacker’s model that the activity was unauthorized.

Context bombs

Content placed in a decoy can be designed to trigger an attacking model’s guardrails and interrupt its work. Tracebit tested the technique in a controlled environment; effectiveness may vary across models and operators.

Observation before blocking

One team described monitoring an attacker and patching what it probed before blocking. This gave defenders more information, though the decision to continue observing depends on visibility and the risk of ongoing harm.

AI infrastructure monitoring

Monitor AI service usage and spend for signs of credential misuse or unauthorized inference, and investigate anomalies alongside identity and resource activity.

Observability as early warning

While AOFs stay loud, application and infrastructure observability telemetry may show the first signs of their activity.

Deception durability

Expect current techniques to lose effectiveness as frameworks adapt. Design deception to change in step with AOFs. Tripwires and deliberate misrouting should not depend on the attacker’s model obeying a message. For example, recent research showed that routing ARTEX to an isolated shadow copy cut successful compromises from 50% to 0%. The exploit still worked on the shadow copy in about half the runs, so the attack was redirected, not stopped.

New risks:

Theft of AI service credentials, which may also pay for attacker inference:

AI gateways and cyber-capable model access concentrate keys, so treat them as tier 0 and prefer workload identity federation to API keys.

Manipulation of defensive AI through planted claims of authorization:

Operators plant markers that tell a defender's AI to triage the activity as an authorized test. Keep a register of approved tests, and check any claimed authorization against it.

Re-entry after partial remediation:

Some AOFs recreated accounts as soon as they were deleted or disabled. Attackers also went after source control tokens so they could push code. Rotate those tokens during remediation and alert on pushes from new identities. Persistence also came from new credentials added to existing OAuth applications.

Multi-target activity:

A responder investigating an attack reported finding evidence that the same attacker was already active inside two other organizations.

Downstream and third-party exposure:

Salesforce reported a credential-driven campaign with signs of AI assistance that targeted customer Salesforce environments through compromised application credentials and trusted integration sessions. Attackers used configured integrations to reach connected services and deployed custom code to support continued access.

Expectations and considerations:

Slow campaigns

No AOF-run slow campaign has been observed yet, and a working one would likely be built to stay unobserved. Human-run activities provide insight on how this evolution could occur: Volt Typhoon kept a foothold in some victim IT environments for at least five years (AA24-038A).

Operational technology

Public testing by Dragos shows frontier models mapping industrial ranges and finding new flaws, and authorized testing knocked a controller offline.

Defensive tooling may not scale to AOF volume

Logging pipelines, case management, SOAR, and other products and services can fail or throttle. Test your controls under load and check the contract terms. Keep a recovery plan for them and a tested out-of-band channel.

Compromised tooling

A fork changed one line of its Docker Compose file to pull a backdoored ARTEX image, so the source code looked clean. The image was pulled about 9,000 times, and 62 internet-facing consoles served it between November 2 and 4.

Notification deadlines

Privileged access in under three hours means regulatory and contractual deadlines can start before the organization knows what was taken. Exfiltration without a staging archive makes scoping harder. Pre-built data-to-system maps and pre-determined notification decision paths for each regime and major contract could prove useful.

VI. Updated Risk Register and Controls List

Table 1 updates the risk register from The AI Vulnerability Storm. Table 2 lists the controls, with a start time for each.

SEVERITY:

CRITICAL
seen in these campaigns and, on its own, leads to privileged access or leaves defenders unable to respond.
HIGH
seen and makes an attack easier or worse, or not yet seen but severe if it happens.
MEDIUM
limited new evidence, and a failure would be contained.
LOW
little change since the last paper. "Validated" means community members or public reporting described at least one case consistent with the risk. It is not a measured rate.

Frontier Ready IDs refer to the expanded edition of the CSA Frontier Ready Maturity Model.

VII. Board Recommendations

The message for the board:

AI-run intrusion campaigns are now cheap, fast, and within reach of criminals with few resources. The security organization that is already funded still holds. What has to change is how fast the organization can decide and act. That takes six decisions that only the board or executive committee can make.

Decisions the board needs to make:

Containment authority

Pre-approve the actions the security team can take without case-by-case sign-off, up to shutting down compromised production systems. Record the approval in the minutes, and name an alternate for each decision-maker.

Disruption tolerance

Accept that fast, automated containment will sometimes hit the wrong system, and set how much disruption each critical service can absorb, and for how long.

Agentic decisions

Consider what decisions agents can make, how we build the guardrails to allow agents to make these decisions, and expect these to continuously require updating.

Notification

Agree in advance who decides when to notify under each regulation and each major contract, because deadlines can start before the scope of a breach is known.

Speed

Approve a buying process that can adopt a new defense within 2-4 weeks.

Funding

Fund AI agents for the security team and access to cyber-ready AI models, with a fallback in case a provider's model declines security work.

Questions the board should ask:

How long would it take us to contain a confirmed intrusion? Some of these attacks reached privileged (administrator-level) access in under three hours.

What can the security team do today without waiting for approval?

Who is accountable if automated containment takes down the wrong system, and how will our insurer treat it?

Which vendors have access to our environment, and how fast can we cut them off?

Have we run one of these attack frameworks against our own environment in a safe test, and what did it find?

Could we handle two serious incidents at the same time?

After an incident, how do we know the attacker is fully removed from our environment?

VIII. Call to Industry

  • Security vendors must prepare for many of their customers facing AOF attacks at the same time. Services need to scale and stay available, especially for customers in an active incident.
  • Security vendors must also prepare to be attacked. They need a tested ability to detect, contain, recover, and tell customers what the impact is.
  • Platforms should give customers ways to slow automated activity (e.g., per-tenant rate and concurrency limits, with checkpoints for unusual behavior).
  • Vendors should document which services must be internet-exposed and give customers controls to scope, monitor, and quickly revoke application and agent access. Support short-lived credentials and workload identity where possible, alongside source restrictions appropriate to the environment.

IX. Open Questions

How quickly will the current limits weaken, and when will a prompt replace the need for an AOF?

As human decisions become untenable for incident response, where does human approval belong in new agentic decision-making loops, especially considering privacy law may require human review of automated decisions?

How do we determine the architecture and design that reduce dependence on patch speed, and how do we implement them?

What is the minimum workable program for an organization with no SOC, where EDR in block mode is the only response that acts without waiting for a person?

How would evidence that AOFs can reliably chain vulnerabilities change exploit maturity ratings and remediation priorities?

Are slow campaigns already running undetected, and do fast campaigns hand access to slower, more methodical groups?

How can defenders and model providers identify, escalate, and resolve recurring refusals of legitimate security work while preserving appropriate safeguards?

When will AOFs be able to cause a chosen physical effect in OT?

How long will AI-aware deception last, and how do we ensure legitimate agent activity isn’t affected?

Who is liable when automated containment takes down the wrong thing, including a false positive that the attacker set up? How will insurers treat this?

What are the updated requirements for a managed security provider, including defensive use of frontier models, and closer integration beyond log triage?

X. Summary

While some of these campaigns discovered and exploited vulnerabilities, most of them relied on known techniques, and their reconnaissance was noisy enough to be detected. What has changed is cost and reach. A downloadable framework and an estimated $145 to $1,500 in AI model fees put a full intrusion campaign within reach of criminals with few resources. The FBI describes some intrusions that reached privileged access in under three hours.

We fully expect upcoming models to remove the need for a specific AOF for the level of sophistication these frameworks currently show, and decrease the time required to reach compromise.

The hardest gaps on the defending side are organizational: response teams built for one incident facing attacks across several sites at once, approval chains that still require human sign-off, and buying processes that cannot adopt a new defense within 2-4 weeks.

Closing these gaps means making decisions about authority, budget, and process, and which of these can be delegated to agents. That work belongs to business leadership alongside the security organization.

Keep in mind these three lessons from community members who faced these attacks:

  • Teams that used AI agents throughout their work kept pace, and others described being overwhelmed.
  • Deception slowed or stopped attackers.
  • Partial cleanup failed. Organizations that remediated only part of a compromise were re-compromised within hours.
